MATCH SCORE: 4

KEY FEATURES: three-tier wireless topology + pre-paired links + range-extender relay + magnetic (AMR) sensor + actuator stroke sensing

OVERLAP:
- [0022]/[0024] — A vehicle area network (VAN 101) is a wireless system linking hubs, range extenders and sensors, i.e. a multi-level wireless architecture.
- [0028]/[0049] — Wireless hub 130a-d acts as the central access point of each subnetwork, functionally the "base wireless device".
- [0030] — A range-extender transmitter/receiver 170a is paired with sensor 110a and communicates with the tractor hub 130a: an intermediate "remote wireless device" between base and sensor.
- [0037] — The transmitter/receiver receives measured data from one or more sensors and reports that data to the local hub wirelessly (sensor↔remote and remote↔base wireless links).
- [0038] — Pairing of sensor 110b, transmitter/receiver 170b and hub 130b can be accomplished in advance during assembly by a technician using pairing device 275.
- [0034] — Tractor hub 130a is paired to trailer hub 130b via an out-of-band link sharing an AES-128 key (base-level link pre-paired).
- [0026]/[0052]/[0059] — Different frequency bands/protocols are used on different links (WiFi 2.4 GHz, 802.15.4 Thread, 433 MHz sub-GHz) — but for communication, not power.
- [0093]/[0094] — An air brake chamber 1212 (pneumatic actuator) drives pushrod 1208; the sensor measures target-vs-sense-element position and this is used to calculate chamber stroke.
- [0085] / claim 10 — Sense element 822 is an anisotropic magnetoresistive (AMR) sensor on a PCB detecting the field of magnet 826 — a magnetic sensor element.

CANDIDATE EVIDENCE:
- [0030]: The tractor subnetwork includes a range-extender transmitter/receiver 170a paired with sensor 110a to relay sensor data to hub 130a, giving the base–remote–sensor three-tier chain.
- [0038]: Sensor, transmitter/receiver and hub can be paired in advance during assembly with a pairing device, matching "pairing performed in advance" on both links.
- [0094]: The sense element 1322 on the fixed brake-chamber bracket and target 1324 on the pushrod measure relative position, which is used to calculate brake-chamber stroke.
- [0085]: The sensor assembly uses an anisotropic magnetoresistive element sensing a magnet's field — the sensor element is a magnetic sensor.
- [0065]/[0109]: Sensors are battery powered with efficient power usage for long life; no wireless/microwave power transfer to sensors or range extenders is disclosed.

DIFFERENCES:
- Benchmark's characterizing feature — a first wireless power supply device beaming microwave power to the sensor device — is absent; candidate sensors are battery powered ([0065], [0110]).
- Benchmark's second wireless power supply device feeding the remote wireless device by microwave is absent; the transmitter/receiver 170 is battery or 12/24 V wired powered ([0057]).
- Benchmark requires the two microwave power frequencies to differ (920 MHz / 2.4 GHz / 5.7 GHz per claim 10); candidate only differentiates *communication* bands ([0052], [0059]), never power-transfer frequencies.
- Benchmark's multi-antenna power transmission, fieldbus-connected computer and direct sensor-to-base branch (benchmark claims 2–3) have no counterpart; candidate's hub/CAN bus [0053] is a different arrangement.
- Benchmark is production-equipment/actuator oriented (claim 4); candidate is entirely vehicle brake-wear oriented ([0011]), where the "actuator" is an air brake chamber.
- Candidate adds brake-pad thickness algorithms, s-cam angle math and temperature anomaly detection ([0105], [0119]) with no benchmark counterpart.

VERDICT: The candidate independently discloses the benchmark's wireless topology (base hub → pre-paired range extender → pre-paired sensor), a magnetic (AMR) sensor element, and stroke sensing of a pneumatic actuator, so the preamble features line up well. However, it discloses nothing about microwave wireless power supply at all — neither the first nor the second power supply device, and therefore not the distinguishing "different microwave frequencies" limitation, which is the entire characterizing portion of benchmark claim 1. It is a relevant partial-overlap reference for the topology and sensing side, but cannot anticipate the benchmark's core solution.

MATCH SCORE: 4

KEY FEATURES: wireless base unit + intermediate repeater field unit + RF wireless power supply + distinct power frequencies + fieldbus-connected control equipment

OVERLAP:
- [0028] / claim 53 — A system of wireless base units (102a-c) wirelessly coupled to wireless field units (104a-g), each field unit coupled to a field device (sensor), i.e. a base/remote/sensor-like three-tier arrangement.
- [0048], [0062] — A wireless field unit acts as a repeater, receiving power and data from a base unit and retransmitting both to another, too-distant wireless field unit; this mirrors the benchmark's base→remote→sensor relay topology.
- [0022], [0051] — The base unit transmits power wirelessly using radio-frequency electromagnetic waves while simultaneously exchanging data over wireless links (RF power supply, comparable to microwave power supply).
- [0059]–[0063] — The wireless field unit has a wireless power/data receiver and a rectenna, i.e. an RF-power-harvesting remote node with no battery or wiring.
- [0052], [0091], claim 25 — Different frequency signals carry different power levels/transmissions; a base unit may instruct neighboring base units which frequency to use when several supply power to the same node.
- [0036] — The base units may be Fieldbus-compliant and communicate with controllers over digital data busses (cf. benchmark claim 3's fieldbus-connected computer).
- [0026], [0075] — Each field unit has a unique ID/security key used to route and encrypt power and data exclusively to that designated unit (a weak analogue of pre-established pairing).

CANDIDATE EVIDENCE:
- [0048]: "Each of the wireless field units 104a-g is configured to operate as a repeater to retransmit power and information received from one of the wireless base units to another one of the wireless field units" ⚠ — discloses base → intermediate node → end node relay of both power and data.
- [0091]: The base unit "may also transmit to each of the selected neighboring wireless base units a frequency value indicating a frequency at which to transmit a power signal to the wireless field unit" — multiple wireless power sources operating on assigned, distinct frequencies.
- [0052]: The transmitter "may be configured to transmit each of a plurality of different power levels via a respective one of a plurality of different frequency signals," including a fixed low-power wake-up frequency separate from the main power link frequency.
- [0022]: Field devices powered wirelessly may be "a temperature sensor, a pressure sensor, a status (open/closed) sensor, an actuator, etc." — an actuator is named as a wirelessly powered field device, but only as a load, with no stroke-position sensing.
- [0026]: Each wireless field unit is associated with a unique ID/security key or code used to encrypt and route power and data exclusively to that designated unit.

DIFFERENCES:
- Benchmark requires the sensor device to output a signal corresponding to the stroke position of an actuator; the candidate never discloses stroke/position detection — an actuator appears only as a powered load ([0022]).
- Benchmark requires a magnetic sensor as the sensor element; the candidate lists only temperature, pressure, level and open/closed sensors ([0028], [0022]) — no magnetic sensor anywhere.
- Benchmark uses two *separate* wireless power supply devices, one dedicated to the sensor device and one to the remote wireless device, on *mutually different* frequencies; the candidate's multiple base units transmit to the *same* field unit for redundancy/summing ([0079], [0091]) — the frequency distinction is per-redundant-link, not per-hierarchy-level.
- Benchmark's three tiers are three distinct device classes (base / remote / sensor) with the sensor communicating wirelessly to the remote; in the candidate the field device is wired ("electrically and communicatively coupled", [0024]) to its field unit, and the relay is field-unit-to-field-unit, i.e. same device class.

- Benchmark's application is production equipment / actuator monitoring; the candidate's is chemical/petroleum process control ([0002]).

However, it lacks every one of the benchmark's characterizing limitations: no dedicated second power supply device for the intermediate node on a *different* frequency from the sensor's supply, no stroke-position output, and no magnetic sensor element. The harvested energy by devices 282 and 284 can be used to recharge the battery"; [0193]: a WiFi router or Bluetooth network signal is harvested by patch device 256 to recharge its battery.

- [0172] — Patch/skin device 282 transmits a 915 MHz ISM signal that battery-less screw 274 rectifies and stores to power its electronics and sensors, i.e. wireless power supply to the sensor device.

KEY FEATURES: microwave wireless power supply + multiple powered devices + different frequencies per device + transmitter–receiver pairing + wirelessly powered factory sensors

OVERLAP:
- Microwave wireless power supply to devices — claim 6 / claim 8 / claim 17: the electromagnetic power transmission signal is a microwave; description states 5.8 GHz is the preferred power-transmission frequency and any frequency above 100 MHz may be used.
- Two (or more) separately powered receiving devices fed at *different* microwave frequencies — claim 1 and claim 12: the transmitter sends a second signal at a second frequency to the first mobile receiver and a third signal at a third frequency to the second mobile receiver, "wherein the second frequency and the third frequency are different"; claim 2/claim 13 add that the two differing-frequency signals may be transmitted simultaneously.
- Multiple frequencies used deliberately so power delivery is not interrupted — description (retuning section): "the array/receiver can use more than one frequency … while one frequency is tuned, the other frequency can continue transmitting power".
- Pairing between the power supply side and the device it supplies — description (power-transmission-technique section): transmitters "can be 'paired' with the devices they should supply", so that neighbours do not unintentionally borrow power; receivers also "lock" onto a single transmitter after negotiation.
- Side communication link separate from the power beam — description (first embodiment): a communication channel 110a is opened between the system 100a and the power receiver 330b "at a frequency other than the frequency used to propagate power", over which the receiver reports received signal strength (claim 7 restates this as the power-meter/control-logic feedback path).
- Sensor devices in production/manufacturing equipment supplied wirelessly — description (application examples): manufacturing plants use large numbers of sensors and controllers that still need power cords despite wireless communication, and "wireless power can be provided to these devices by incorporating one of the wireless power receivers described above".
- Distributed multiple power-transmitting arrays, master/slave organised — description (separate-arrays section): individual array units synchronise their base signal clocks from a designated "master" unit, allowing multiple arrays distributed around a building, manufacturing plant or office.

CANDIDATE EVIDENCE:
- claim 1: A microwave power transmitter transmits a second power signal at a second frequency to a first mobile receiver and a third power signal at a third frequency to a second mobile receiver, the second and third frequencies being different.
- claim 6: The electromagnetic power transmission signal is a microwave.
- claim 7: The receiver has a rectifier and power meter that measures received power strength and transmits that indication back to the transmitter, which uses it to select the transmission frequency.
- Description, manufacturing-plant application example: factory sensors and controllers that already communicate wirelessly still need power cords, so they are to be powered by one of the disclosed wireless (microwave) power receivers.
- Description, pairing/priority section: transmitters can be "paired" with the specific devices they are to supply, and a receiver locks onto a single transmitter.

DIFFERENCES:
- The benchmark's three-tier communication architecture — base wireless device ↔ remote wireless device ↔ sensor device, with the remote device relaying sensor signals — is absent; the candidate has only transmitter ↔ receiver links plus master/slave clock synchronisation between arrays.
- Benchmark requires pre-established (pre-paired) *communication* links on both hops; the candidate's pairing is between a power transmitter and the device it powers, not a two-hop data relay chain.
- Benchmark requires two physically distinct wireless power supply devices (20A to the sensor, 20B to the remote device); the candidate's differing frequencies come from one phased-array transmitter serving two mobile receivers.
- Benchmark's sensor outputs a signal corresponding to an actuator stroke position — nothing comparable in the candidate.
- Benchmark's sensor element is a magnetic sensor; the candidate's only named sensing element is a motion sensor/accelerometer (receivers 1100/1200) used for radiation safety, not magnetic position sensing.

MATCH SCORE: 4

KEY FEATURES: two-tier wireless power supply + microwave power transmission + Bluetooth pairing in advance + different power frequencies + master/slave wireless hierarchy

OVERLAP:
- **Three-tier wireless topology (base → intermediate → end device)** — [0040]/[0043]: a dedicated wireless power feeding device 51 or 5G radio base station 52 supplies the master portable terminal A0, which in turn radiates power to slave terminals A1/A2; A0 acts as the intermediate "relay" node, structurally analogous to the benchmark's remote wireless device between base and sensor.
- **Wireless communication link between the upper node and the intermediate node** — [0047]: the first and second communicators of A0 perform wireless communication with a mobile-communication-system base station (5G), and [0076] A0 searches for and communicates with the dedicated wireless power feeding device.
- **Wireless communication link between the intermediate node and the end devices** — [0041]/[0042]: A0 controls A1/A2 through inter-device communication 31, 32 using Bluetooth.
- **Pairing performed in advance on the upper link** — [0079]: power reception begins only "after pairing with the wireless base station or the found wireless power feeding device is completed."
- **Pairing performed in advance on the lower link** — [0042]: group membership between A0 and A1/A2 is determined by whether Bluetooth pairing has been performed.
- **Wireless power supply to the end device using microwaves** — [0047]/[0050]: the power transmission control circuit draws power from the battery and radiates electromagnetic waves via the microwave-band (or millimeter-wave) communicators to feed A1.
- **Wireless power supply to the intermediate node using microwaves** — [0043]: A0 receives electromagnetic waves 61, 62 from the dedicated wireless power feeding device 51 and the 5G base station and is thereby charged.
- **Different microwave frequencies used on the two power-supply links** — [0132]/[0138]: the dedicated feeder 1800 transmits at frequency fA to A0 and fB to B0, and A0 then re-transmits power to C1 on the *other* frequency fB, i.e. the frequency feeding the intermediate node differs from the frequency it uses to feed the downstream terminal.
- **Frequency-band selection/antenna switching per power link** — [0078]/[0139]: the antenna control unit confirms the frequency used for wireless power feeding and switches the antenna switch to the power reception or power transmission circuit for that frequency band.

CANDIDATE EVIDENCE:
- [0043] — A dedicated wireless power feeding device 51 and a 5G radio base station 52 both wirelessly supply power to the master portable terminal A0 via electromagnetic waves 61, 62.
- [0050] — A0's power transmission control circuit takes power from its battery and radiates electromagnetic waves from the microwave/millimeter-wave communicators to supply power to the slave terminal A1.
- [0042] — Inter-device communication between A0 and its slaves uses Bluetooth, and group membership is established by prior pairing.
- [0138] — Power transmission from A0 to C1 deliberately uses frequency fB while the dedicated feeder supplies A0 at frequency fA, so the two power-feed links occupy different frequencies without interfering.
- [0079] — Power reception by A0 starts only after pairing with the base station or the discovered wireless power feeding device is completed.

DIFFERENCES:
- The benchmark's end node is a **sensor device outputting a signal corresponding to the stroke position of an actuator**; the candidate's end nodes are consumer wearables (wireless headset, smart watch) — [0041]. No actuator, no stroke position anywhere.
- The benchmark requires the sensor element to include a **magnetic sensor**; the candidate mentions only a generic internal "sensor 106" in the terminal's block diagram ([0045]) with no type and no measurement function.
- The benchmark is an **industrial/production-equipment** system (fieldbus, computer, production equipment, plural sensors per actuator); the candidate has no factory context — its problem is sharing wireless-charging resources among consumer terminals ([0009]).
- In the benchmark the two wireless power supply devices are **separate dedicated devices (20A/20B)** feeding sensor and remote respectively; in the candidate the "first" feeder is the portable terminal A0 itself (a battery-powered relay), not a dedicated power supply device.
- The benchmark's frequency difference is an intrinsic architectural requirement tied to the two feeder devices; the candidate's frequency difference (fA/fB) arises from inter-group interference avoidance and spectrum re-use ([0138]), a different rationale.
- The benchmark specifies 920 MHz / 2.4 GHz / 5.7 GHz bands (claim 10) and multi-antenna feeding (claim 2); the candidate names only generic microwave/millimeter-wave bands ([0047]).

OVERLAP:
- **Wireless power supply between two devices** — [0034]: a power transmission device 10 wirelessly supplies power to a plurality of power receiving devices 20 (benchmark likewise has power supply devices 20A/20B feeding sensor/remote devices).
- **Wireless communication accompanying the power link** — [0034]/[0054]: the transmission and receiving devices exchange the data required for power supply over a packet/frame-format wireless link.
- **Advance association/identification before the link is used** — [0051] and [0068]–[0071]: an "association period" in which the transmitter requests a device ID, the receiver returns it, and the ID is registered in a management table before power transmission starts; this is a loose analogue of the benchmark's "pairing performed in advance".

CANDIDATE EVIDENCE:
- [0004] — The disclosure is explicitly about electromagnetic-induction / magnetic-field-resonance / electric-field-coupling / radio-wave contactless power systems, with magnetic field resonance chosen as the embodiment; no microwave power beaming is claimed or described.
